name: rust-phf (compile-time perfect hash maps)
baseline: std::collections::HashMap (Rust) populated at program startup from parsed/bundled data
workload: Initializing the conduit-mime-types crate's filename-extension-to-MIME-type lookup table at program startup: before, parsing bundled JSON at runtime and inserting into a HashMap; after, using phf_codegen to emit a compile-time-generated perfect hash map, so the initialization step becomes essentially free.
claimed_speedup: "This step resulted in a roughly 80% performance improvement" for the table-initialization step; initialization time described as reduced to "essentially zero" (verbatim-ish, methodology and exact metric otherwise unstated)
stars_or_usage: 2.2k stars; used in production by crates.io (conduit-mime-types crate)
tradeoffs: Map is immutable once built (must regenerate to add/remove keys); requires a build-time codegen step (phf_codegen) or macro; keys/set must be known at compile time; a separate Rust forum thread (users.rust-lang.org, "Why is phf::Map slower than std HashMap?") reports phf::Map losing to std HashMap for some small/medium key counts at pure lookup time, so the win is mainly on initialization/startup cost rather than guaranteed steady-state lookup latency.
caveats: First-party engineering-blog write-up (Mainmatter/Tobias Bieniek, 2022-06-23), no hardware, compiler, or exact timing numbers given -- only the "~80%" figure and qualitative "essentially zero" claim for the initialization step; not a controlled microbenchmark against std::collections::HashMap, and not compared against C++ std::unordered_map at all (Rust-only). Capped at tier C for missing methodology.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch "Rust phf crate benchmark vs HashMap blog post static perfect hash faster" -> https://mainmatter.com/blog/2022/06/23/the-perfect-hash-function/
